column1: owner-compensation-review|owner compensation review|The owner’s work, pay arrangements, and cash needs should be described before a provider proposes compensation-related work. Ask how the analysis will be documented and coordinated with payroll rather than requesting a number in isolation.|owner duties; payroll history; distribution records|Who reviews the owner’s responsibilities?; What assumptions are documented?; Who implements an agreed payroll change?|a written compensation review scope with responsible parties|Business and owner

first-payroll-handoff|first owner payroll handoff|A new payroll process needs an operational handoff as well as analysis. Identify the payroll provider, information required, implementation date, and the person who checks the first reporting cycle.|payroll provider details; owner role summary; implementation date|Who supplies payroll instructions?; Who checks the first payroll reports?; Which registrations and recurring tasks are included?|an implementation responsibility map|Business and owner

entity-structure-review|entity structure review before expansion|Start with a complete entity map and the commercial reason for the proposed change. A provider’s recommendation should distinguish financial modeling, legal work, filings, and the responsibilities that follow the change.|entity agreements; ownership chart; expansion plan|Which alternatives will be modeled?; Which legal work is outside scope?; Who updates the books after implementation?|an alternatives review and entity responsibility map|Business and owner

adding-a-business-partner|adding a business partner|A proposed ownership change should be reviewed before its commercial terms become binding. Gather the current agreements and intended economics, then ask which questions require coordinated tax and legal analysis.|ownership agreements; proposed terms; contribution details|When should counsel join the process?; Who models the proposed economics?; How are implementation documents and filings assigned?|a partner-entry review timetable|Ownership changes

partner-buyout|buying out a business partner|The commercial terms of a buyout may change during negotiation. Ask for an engagement that identifies who updates the analysis when price, payment timing, or the ownership arrangement changes.|buyout outline; ownership records; financing terms|Who reviews changed deal terms?; Which valuation work is separate?; What information is needed before a binding agreement?|a buyout diligence and coordination brief|Ownership changes

family-ownership-transition|family business ownership transition|A family transition involves business continuity and the interests of several people. Explain the intended roles, timing, and ownership goals. Ask the advisor to separate its analysis from legal documentation and valuation work.|family ownership map; role summary; transition goals|Which family members are covered by the scope?; Who coordinates valuation and legal documents?; How are decisions and assumptions recorded?|a family-transition responsibility and decision calendar|Ownership changes

minority-investor-entry|bringing in a minority investor|An investment proposal changes ownership economics and may introduce reporting or consent obligations. Bring the actual proposed terms and ask which modeling, documentation, and specialist work the engagement would cover.|term sheet; capitalization table; existing agreements|Which terms must be modeled before signing?; Who reviews investor reporting requirements?; How are later changes in the term sheet handled?|an investor-entry review checklist|Ownership changes

cofounder-equity-reorganization|reorganizing cofounder equity|Reallocating ownership is a specific transaction rather than a general planning label. Explain the commercial reason, existing interests, and proposed change so candidates can identify the facts and professionals needed.|current equity records; proposed allocation; founder agreements|Who confirms the starting ownership records?; Which legal and valuation work is needed?; Who checks the completed records against the agreed terms?|an equity-change review and handoff plan|Ownership changes

business-acquisition-diligence|tax diligence before a business acquisition|Acquisition work should be tied to an actual target, transaction structure, and timetable. Ask what the provider will examine, which information it needs, and how findings will reach the negotiating team.|letter of intent; target financials; diligence request list|Which tax records will be reviewed?; Who communicates issues to counsel?; What happens if the transaction structure changes?|a transaction-specific diligence scope|Transactions

asset-purchase-review|reviewing a proposed business asset purchase|An asset purchase requires a clear inventory of what is being bought and who will own it. Ask for analysis based on the purchase documents and how the final agreed terms will be handed to the accounting team.|purchase outline; asset list; financing terms|Which purchase documents are required?; Who reviews the final allocation documents?; Who enters acquired assets into the records?|an asset-purchase review and accounting handoff|Transactions

business-sale-readiness|preparing a business for sale|Sale preparation begins before a final buyer proposal. Describe the expected timing and available records. Ask which work can help organize the financial and ownership information that a transaction team will need.|ownership records; financial statements; expected sale timeline|Which records should be reconciled first?; Who coordinates with the transaction attorney?; What deliverables are useful before a buyer is selected?|a sale-readiness record and decision plan|Transactions

seller-financing-review|evaluating seller financing|Payment timing, credit risk, and contract terms belong in the same transaction discussion. Ask which alternatives the advisor will compare and which assumptions require input from counsel or a financing professional.|proposed note terms; payment schedule; transaction outline|How are alternative payment terms compared?; Who reviews credit and legal questions?; Who updates the analysis after negotiations?|a documented payment-structure comparison|Transactions

earnout-negotiation|reviewing an earnout before signing|An earnout depends on defined performance measures and a future calculation process. Provide the draft terms and ask who reviews their financial assumptions, reporting requirements, and interaction with the wider transaction.|draft earnout terms; performance definitions; reporting outline|Who checks the financial measurement assumptions?; Which contract terms require counsel?; Who handles later calculation or reporting questions?|an earnout review with assigned follow-up responsibilities|Transactions

acquisition-integration|coordinating tax work after an acquisition|Closing a transaction does not finish the record handoff. Ask who connects closing documents, the accounting records, payroll, and future filings, and who confirms that the assigned tasks are complete.|closing documents; opening balance records; integration task list|Who receives the closing package?; Who reconciles the opening records?; Which post-close tasks are included in the fee?|a post-acquisition implementation tracker|Transactions

commercial-property-purchase|buying a commercial property|A property purchase may involve an operating company, a property entity, financing, and separate specialists. Describe those relationships before requesting a proposal and identify the decisions still open.|purchase contract; property details; financing proposal|Which entities are covered?; Who reviews records before a specialist study is proposed?; How will the work reach the return preparer?|a property-purchase review scope|Property and assets

first-rental-property|adding a first rental property to a business owner’s plan|A first property can introduce records and responsibilities that differ from the operating business. Explain how it will be owned and operated, and ask who coordinates the property information with the owner’s existing tax work.|ownership proposal; operating budget; property records|What records should begin at acquisition?; Which return and entity responsibilities are covered?; Who coordinates with the existing preparer?|a first-property documentation and advisory brief|Property and assets

portfolio-record-review|reviewing a rental portfolio’s records|A portfolio review should make property-level information usable. Ask how the provider will identify missing schedules, reconcile ownership, and coordinate any separately scoped specialist work.|property inventory; depreciation schedules; prior returns|Who identifies missing property records?; How are entity and property schedules reconciled?; Which studies or filings need separate scope?|a property-by-property record gap assessment|Property and assets

cost-segregation-coordination|coordinating cost segregation with a tax preparer|A specialist report needs an assigned review and filing handoff. Ask the candidate to distinguish the study itself, analysis of how it fits your facts, and preparation of any required reporting.|property details; existing asset schedules; proposed study scope|Who reviews the study in context?; Who prepares any related filings?; How are fees and implementation responsibilities separated?|a study-to-return coordination plan|Property and assets

property-disposition-review|reviewing a planned property sale|A disposition review needs the property’s history and the intended transaction terms. Ask how the advisor will gather schedules, review alternatives, and coordinate with the people completing the sale.|asset history; depreciation schedules; proposed sale terms|Which historical records are needed?; When should the review occur?; Who updates the analysis if the sale terms change?|a sale review and document timetable|Property and assets

sale-leaseback-evaluation|evaluating a sale and leaseback|A sale and leaseback connects property ownership with the operating company’s future commitments. Ask for analysis of the actual proposed arrangements and coordination with legal and financing specialists.|proposed sale terms; draft lease; entity map|Which ongoing lease assumptions are modeled?; Who reviews related entity arrangements?; What specialist work is separately engaged?|a combined property and operating-company review brief|Property and assets

equipment-purchase-timing|reviewing equipment purchase timing|The review should start with the business need, purchase commitments, financing, and expected use. Ask how the provider separates the operating decision from any tax analysis and documents the assumptions used.|equipment quote; financing options; planned use date|Which purchase and use facts must be confirmed?; Who compares financing alternatives?; Who maintains the completed asset records?|a purchase decision and record handoff worksheet|Property and assets

lease-versus-buy|comparing equipment leasing and purchasing|Compare the actual agreements rather than only monthly payments. Ask who reviews ownership, payment timing, ongoing obligations, and the complete cost assumptions used in the analysis.|lease proposal; purchase quote; service obligations|What costs are included in each alternative?; Which contract terms need legal review?; Who records the final arrangement?|a documented lease and purchase comparison|Property and assets

fleet-expansion|planning a business vehicle fleet expansion|A fleet decision involves ownership, financing, use records, and operating capacity. Describe how vehicles will be used and ask who maintains the documentation after the decision.|vehicle list; financing proposals; use policies|Which use records are required?; Who coordinates payroll or policy questions?; How are additions and disposals tracked?|a fleet documentation and review plan|Property and assets

new-location|opening a new business location|A new location changes operating costs, commitments, and reporting needs. Bring the location budget and proposed agreements, then ask how the advisor coordinates entity, filing, and bookkeeping questions.|location budget; lease proposal; staffing plan|Which jurisdiction questions need review?; Who creates location-level reporting?; How are startup and ongoing tasks assigned?|a new-location advisory and reporting checklist|Growth and operations

second-state|expanding into a second state|Identify where work, people, property, and customers will be located. Ask the candidate to evaluate the actual facts and define the jurisdictions and filings inside the engagement.|activity map; staffing plan; sales channels|Which facts are needed to review state obligations?; Who handles registrations and filings?; What triggers a new scope when activities change?|a jurisdiction review and implementation brief|Growth and operations

remote-team-expansion|hiring a remote team across states|Remote hiring requires a reliable inventory of where people work and who maintains that information. Ask which payroll, tax, and legal questions are included and which require separate specialists.|worker locations; payroll setup; engagement agreements|Who tracks location changes?; Which payroll tasks are included?; Who coordinates employment-law questions?|a remote-work information and responsibility map|Growth and operations

contractor-team-review|reviewing contractor arrangements with a tax team|Describe the actual working arrangements and contracts. Ask which questions belong to tax, payroll, and legal specialists, and how the review will distinguish analysis from implementation.|contractor agreements; payment ledger; work descriptions|Which facts need legal or payroll review?; Who documents conclusions and assumptions?; Who implements any agreed operational changes?|a coordinated contractor-arrangement review brief|Growth and operations

outsourced-cfo-handoff|coordinating a tax advisor with an outsourced CFO|An additional advisor should have a clear place in the existing team. Ask who owns forecasting, book adjustments, planning recommendations, and filing handoffs so work is neither assumed nor duplicated.|current service scopes; reporting calendar; contact map|Which work stays with the CFO?; Who produces tax projections?; How are decisions and completed actions communicated?|a finance-team responsibility matrix|Team coordination

bookkeeping-cleanup|organizing books before a tax planning engagement|A planning proposal should identify whether the records are usable and who corrects gaps. Ask for a separate description of cleanup, recurring bookkeeping, and advisory analysis.|trial balance; unreconciled accounts; prior returns|Who assesses record readiness?; Which cleanup work is separately billed?; What must be completed before projections begin?|a record-readiness and cleanup handoff plan|Team coordination

changing-preparers|changing tax preparers without losing continuity|A provider change requires a specific record transfer and deadline plan. Identify open work and ask which firm handles each return, notice, adjustment, and prior-year question.|prior returns; work-in-progress list; filing calendar|Who handles work already in progress?; Which schedules must transfer?; How are open questions resolved between firms?|a preparer-transition checklist|Team coordination

advisory-with-existing-cpa|adding advisory alongside an existing CPA|Explain the planning gap and the current CPA’s scope. Ask candidates to define how analysis, implementation, and filing will be shared before assuming that a new engagement requires replacing the preparer.|existing engagement; decision list; entity map|What remains with the current CPA?; Who implements recommendations?; How will the advisors communicate with permission?|a shared advisory and preparation responsibility map|Team coordination

quarterly-projection-process|setting up a quarterly tax projection process|A recurring projection process needs dependable inputs and a review date. Ask which records are required, which assumptions are refreshed, and who explains changes to the owner.|current books; payment history; income outlook|When must records be available?; Who explains changed assumptions?; Who communicates any agreed payment instructions?|a projection calendar and input checklist|Planning process

cash-reserve-review|coordinating owner cash and tax reserves|The owner’s available cash and the company’s operating needs should be described separately. Ask how the analysis incorporates known commitments, uncertain income, and the responsibilities for updating forecasts.|cash forecast; owner needs; scheduled commitments|Which cash assumptions are documented?; Who updates the forecast?; How are distributions and reserves discussed together?|a cash-assumption and review calendar|Planning process

uneven-income-year|planning advisory work for an uneven income year|One unusually strong or weak period should be explained in context. Bring the reasons for the change and ask how the candidate distinguishes recurring activity from one-time events in its analysis.|monthly financials; unusual transactions; forward budget|Which events are treated as nonrecurring?; When will assumptions be revisited?; Who evaluates changes before the next decision?|an income-change review brief|Planning process

large-contract-win|reviewing the impact of a large new contract|A signed contract may create costs before collections arrive. Ask the advisor to work from the actual contract, expected delivery, and financing needs rather than simply projecting last year’s results upward.|signed contract; delivery budget; collection terms|Which contract assumptions enter the review?; Who updates the cash forecast?; What changes would require additional analysis?|a contract-growth planning and reporting brief|Growth and operations

retirement-plan-coordination|coordinating retirement plan design with an administrator|A plan discussion may require tax analysis, administration, legal input, and employee information. Ask which professionals perform each part and how the decision and implementation timeline are coordinated.|employee roster; compensation records; existing plan documents|Who compares design alternatives?; Who confirms administrator responsibilities?; How are adoption and ongoing tasks tracked?|a plan-design coordination and task map|Benefits and people

employee-benefits-review|reviewing benefits for owners and employees|Describe the actual owners, employees, and existing arrangements. Ask which benefits questions are inside the advisory scope and which require administrators, insurance professionals, or counsel.|benefit summaries; owner relationships; employee roster|Which arrangements are reviewed?; Who supplies specialist analysis?; Who confirms payroll and implementation changes?|a benefits-review scope and handoff checklist|Benefits and people

key-employee-equity|considering equity for a key employee|A proposed incentive arrangement needs analysis of the actual terms and coordination with counsel. Ask which options the provider will evaluate and who handles documents, records, and ongoing reporting.|draft incentive terms; equity records; employee role|Which alternatives will be evaluated?; Who drafts and reviews the documents?; Who maintains the updated ownership records?|an incentive-arrangement coordination brief|Benefits and people

prior-year-record-review|reviewing prior-year returns and supporting records|Define the question that prompts the review and the years involved. Ask the candidate to distinguish an initial review, further analysis, and any separately authorized amendments or representation.|prior returns; supporting schedules; identified questions|Which years and issues are covered?; What triggers additional work?; Who prepares any authorized filings?|a prior-year review scope with escalation steps|Records and filings

notice-response-coordination|coordinating an IRS notice response with an advisor|A notice has a specific issue and deadline. Ask who is responsible for reviewing it, obtaining authorization, preparing a response, and tracking follow-up. Do not assume a general advisory fee includes representation.|notice copy; response deadline; relevant returns|Who is authorized to represent the business?; What response work is included?; How will deadline and follow-up responsibility be recorded?|a notice-response responsibility and deadline plan|Records and filings

extension-season-handoff|coordinating planning during an extended filing season|An extension period can involve unfinished preparation and new business decisions at the same time. Ask who owns each workstream and how draft information will be distinguished from finalized records.|filing calendar; open preparation items; upcoming decisions|Who completes the pending returns?; Which figures remain provisional?; When will the planning analysis be updated?|an extended-season filing and planning handoff|Records and filings

partnership-k1-coordination|coordinating partnership K-1 information|Identify each interest and the team responsible for obtaining and reviewing the records. Ask how incomplete or changing information will be handled and how business and owner work will be coordinated.|ownership interests; available K-1s; missing information list|Who follows up on missing documents?; Which entity and owner work is covered?; Who reconciles later corrections?|a partnership-information collection and review map|Records and filings

business-personal-handoff|connecting business and personal tax planning|Separate the company records, owner records, and shared decisions in the initial brief. Ask which people and entities are covered and who coordinates information across engagements.|entity list; owner summary; current engagement scopes|Which owners are covered?; Who reconciles shared information?; What requires a separate personal engagement?|a business-and-owner engagement boundary map|Business and owner

annual-retainer-comparison|comparing an annual tax retainer with a defined advisory project|Compare the work and support period rather than only the payment schedule. Ask each candidate to show deliverables, meeting cadence, implementation responsibility, exclusions, and the complete project cost.|written proposals; expected support needs; fee schedules|What is delivered during the support period?; Which work requires another fee?; What happens when new questions arise later?|a like-for-like advisory proposal comparison|Choosing a provider
